title: Infections in Solid Organ Transplant Recipients

questions.stem: A 76-year-old man presented with a 2-day history of fever, fatigue, and occasional rigors. He had undergone deceased donor kidney transplantation for polycystic kidney disease 26 years ago and was on azathioprine and prednisone for maintenance immunosuppression. He had had recurrent episodes of fever, rigors, and sepsis for several months with blood cultures positive for Escherichia coli. Investigations: Blood cultures positive for E. coli Urinalysis: +1 protein and trace blood; urine cultures no growth An infected cyst was considered as a potential nidus of relapsing infection
questions.lead_in: What is the most sensitive diagnostic modality to detect cyst infection?

options.text: CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis
MRI of the abdomen and pelvis

questions.explanation: Positron emission tomography scan A large retrospective study performed at a referral center in France showed that PET scan was superior to ultrasound, CT scan, and MRI for the detection of infected cysts.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q38

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man attended for pretravel advice. He had undergone heart transplantation 6 months previously. He was maintained on tacrolimus and prednisone for immunosuppression and had not had any episodes of allograft rejection. He intended to travel to Vellore, India, for 2 weeks and then on to Manila, the Philippines, for 2 weeks before returning home.
questions.explanation: Oral typhoid vaccine Immunosuppressed patients should not receive live vaccines such as BCG, MMR, oral polio, and oral typhoid vaccine. Inactivated vaccines such as influenza, hepatitis A or B, pneumococcal, and adsorbed tetanus vaccine are permitted, although these are less likely to be effective in immunocompromised hosts. Both oral and inactivated polio vaccine offer excellent individual immunity, but the oral vaccine is live and therefore contraindicated in this patient. Routine polio immunizations in both the UK and the United States are given as inactivated polio vaccine (IPV).
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 4 Q41

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man underwent deceased donor kidney transplant for end-stage renal disease secondary to diabetes mellitus. He received antithymocyte globulin for induction and tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisone for maintenance immunosuppression. Investigations: Recipient CMV IgG negative Donor CMV IgG indeterminate
questions.lead_in: What strategy should be recommended to prevent CMV disease?
questions.explanation: Valganciclovir Since the donor had indeterminate CMV serology, and the recipient was CMV seronegative, clinicians should assume that the donor was CMV seropositive since this is the higherrisk possibility and administer prophylaxis accordingly. The standard for CMV D+/R− patients is to administer valganciclovir for 6 months. Valganciclovir is rapidly metabolized to active ganciclovir in the GI tract and liver and may be taken once daily. Use of oral ganciclovir has very low bioavailability and would have a very high pill burden. Foscarnet and cidofovir are only available IV , and their role is for CMV prophylaxis when first-line treatments are contraindicated, or there is resistance. Aciclovir is not active against CMV .
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q25

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman presented with dyspnea associated with nonproductive cough. She rapidly progressed to acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation. She had received an orthotopic liver transplant 3 months previously for cirrhosis due to autoimmune hepatitis. The donor was a 28-year-old man who died after a motor vehicle accident in Minneapolis. Granulomas were noted on histopathology of the transplanted liver. Investigations: CXR: diffuse, bilateral pulmonary infiltrates Serum Aspergillus galactomannan positive with an index of 1.2 (cut-off for positivity ≥0.5) BAL fluid: fungal cultures positive after 17 days. White to brown colonies with a fine cottony texture seen The same organism was recovered from the lysis-centrifugation blood culture
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely pathogen?
questions.explanation: Histoplasma capsulatum The patient has disseminated histoplasmosis, a disease endemic in the midwestern United States. The presence of granulomas in the transplanted liver suggests donor-derived disease which typically occurs in the early posttransplant period as in this case. Galactomannan, a polysaccharide present in the cell wall of several fungi, is released during host infection. Serum galactomannan can be detected in invasive aspergillosis, histoplasmosis, fusariosis, and penicilliosis (but not mucormycosis). In contrast to Aspergillus, Histoplasma may be recovered from blood cultures in cases of disseminated disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q15

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman sought pretravel medical advice. She planned to go to Bolivia for vacation to visit family. She had a history of liver transplantation for Wilson’s disease 6 months prior and was doing well on immunosuppressants. She asked specifically about yellow fever vaccination.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Advise against future travel to Bolivia due to the risk of yellow fever
Counsel against the trip if visiting a high-risk area
Delay the travel plans until she is 2 years post-transplant
Mosquito bite avoidance precautions will suffice

questions.explanation: Counsel against the trip if visiting high-risk area This is an immunocompromised patient planning an elective trip to a country that has yellow fever. Yellow fever is a live vaccine that could cause significant side effects in immunosuppression. Areas with risk for yellow fever are geographically restricted and thus avoided. A review of the specific destinations can inform if the patient will be exposed to yellow fever or not.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q29

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of high-grade fever and chills. He had undergone liver transplantation for primary sclerosing cholangitis 3 weeks earlier. He was maintained on tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisone. Investigations: Recipient CMV IgG negative, donor CMV IgG negative Total white cell count 20.1 ×109/L Alkaline phosphatase 406 IU/L
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Increase immunosuppression for acute cellular rejection
Reduce immunosuppression for drug-induced liver injury
Start empirical ganciclovir for presumed CMV disease
Start empirical ivAB for intraabdominal infection

questions.explanation: Start empirical ivAB for intraabdominal infection Intraabdominal and biliary complications after liver transplant range from biliary leaks and bilomas to ascending cholangitis and liver abscess from biliary strictures resulting from hepatic artery thrombosis. These patients can present without right upper quadrant pain or tenderness because of allograft denervation. CMV disease is unlikely given leukocytosis and D−/R− status, and invasive aspergillosis is unlikely given early presentation posttransplant and the absence of neutropenia. Surgical complication or intraabdominal infection should be suspected, empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics started, and the abdomen imaged.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q24

needs: Chapter 151 — JC, BK, and Other Polyomaviruses
questions.stem: A 51-year-old woman was found to have a raised serum creatinine of 2.5 mg/dL. She had undergone a kidney transplantation 9 months earlier. She was asymptomatic. Her immunosuppressive medications included tacrolimus, mycophenolate, and prednisone. She had normal renal function on previous follow-up visits and had a baseline creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL. No changes were made to her medications recently. Her urinalysis was normal.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: BK virus nephropathy BK virus nephropathy is asymptomatic and should be suspected when there is an unexplained rise in serum creatinine in kidney transplant recipients. The diagnosis is confirmed by the identification of decoy cells in urine cytology and detection of BK virus nucleic acid in urine and blood. Other options listed are typically symptomatic.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q40

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man presented with sudden onset left flank pain, radiating to groin. He had a history of lung transplantation 9 months previously, and cerebral toxoplasmosis 3 weeks earlier. He was taking cyclosporine, prednisone, fluconazole, valganciclovir, sulfadiazine, and pyrimethamine. Investigations: Urine dipstick 3+ blood CT kidney, ureter, and bladder: 7mm calcific density in the left proximal ureter with associated moderate hydronephrosis. Multiple 1–2 mm nonobstructing calculi also seen in the renal parenchyma
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative medication?
questions.explanation: Sulfadiazine High-dose sulfonamides can cause crystalluria. Some antiretroviral agents can also cause crystalluria, most notably indinavir and atazanavir. Aciclovir is another drug that can be associated with crystalluria.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 3 Q40

questions.question: A patient is awaiting a kidney transplant. He is EBV negative. A donor kidney is available, and the donor's serology is VCA IgM negative, VCA IgG positive, EBNA positive.
questions.question_raw: A patient is awaiting a kidney transplant. He is EBV negative. A donor kidney is available, and the donor's serology is VCA IgM neg, VCA IgG pos, EBNA pos.

parts.text: Interpret the serology.
What are the clinical implications of transplanting into an EBV negative host?

parts_raw.text: Interpret the serology
What are the clinical implications of transplanting into an EBV negative host?

questions.model_answer: a) The donor is a healthy EBV-immune carrier with past (remote) infection, not acute: IgM VCA is negative (IgM VCA appears at presentation and persists only 4-8 weeks in acute infection), while IgG VCA is positive (appears at presentation, lifelong) and EBNA is positive (appears 3-4 weeks after onset, lifelong). Presence of EBNA with absent IgM VCA excludes recent/acute infection and confirms established latency. b) This is an EBV donor-positive/recipient-negative (D+/R-) mismatch. The seronegative recipient is at high risk of primary EBV infection transmitted with the graft under immunosuppression, and therefore at markedly increased risk of post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease (PTLD); up to half of PTLD occurs in the setting of primary EBV infection, and EBV-naive recipients (as with children) are the group at greatest risk. Implication: EBV serostatus monitoring and quantitative EBV viral-load surveillance post-transplant to allow pre-emptive reduction of immunosuppression or rituximab.

questions.question: A 35-year-old male kidney transplant recipient who works as a landscaper presents with a 2-month history of shortness of breath, fever and cough. Physical exam and questionnaire reveal no suspicion of extra-pulmonary disease. You suspect an acute Histoplasma infection. Chest radiograph shows bilateral diffuse micronodular infiltrates.
questions.question_raw: 5. 35 year old male, kidney transplant. He works as a landscaper. He presents with a 2- months history of shortness of breath, fever and cough. Physical exam and questionnaire do not reveal any suspicion of extra-pulmonary disease. You suspect an acute Histoplasma infection. Chest X-ray reveals bilateral diffuse micronodular infiltrates.

parts.text: What infection prevention precautions are required for the nurse tending to the patient on the ward?
What infection prevention precautions are required for the lab tech working on the patient's specimen culture plates?
Apart from culture and histopathology, which other diagnostic test could help in the diagnosis?
Considering the transmission cycle of this organism, how could a healthcare worker acquire infection with this organism?
What are two indications to initiate therapy in this patient?

parts_raw.text: What infection prevention precautions are required for: Nurse tending to the patient on the ward?
What infection prevention precautions are required for: (ii) Lab tech working on the patient's specimen culture plates?
b) Apart from culture and histopathology, which other diagnostic test (1) could help in diagnosis?
c) Considering the transmission cycle of this organism, how would it be possible for a healthcare worker (at large) to get infected with this organism?
d) What are 2 indications to initiate therapy in this patient?

questions.model_answer: a) Routine/standard precautions only – human-to-human transmission of Histoplasma via the pulmonary route has not been reported, so no isolation is required. b) Laboratory biosafety: clinical specimens can be handled with routine practices, but manipulation/propagation of the mycelial (mould) phase is a biohazard and requires Biosafety Level 3 precautions with work in a biological safety cabinet. c) Histoplasma polysaccharide antigen detection in urine and/or serum by EIA (positive in ~70-80% of moderate-severe acute pulmonary disease); H and M precipitin bands and complement-fixation serology are complementary. d) (1) Immunosuppression (transplant recipient) – places him at high risk of progressive disseminated disease. (2) Illness that has not improved after >1 month (his symptoms have persisted ~2 months) or presence of hypoxemia.
questions.beyond_mandell: Immunosuppression as a stand-alone indication to treat acute pulmonary histoplasmosis is emphasized in the IDSA 2007 histoplasmosis guideline; Mandell text explicitly grounds only the '>1 month without improvement or hypoxemia' criterion.

cohort_answer.text: Nurse: Standard precautions. Lab tech: Containment level 3 facility as per PHAC, work under biologic safety cabinet with PPE (e.g. gloves). Other diagnostic test: Histoplasma serum + urinary antigen, serology. Transmission to HCW: If there is construction around the hospital; In lab: Inhalation of conidia spores or accidental parenteral inoculation causing cutaneous infection. Indications to initiate therapy: Bilateral involvement; Immunocompromised; Symptoms >1mo. Tx: AmphoB x1-2 weeks, followed by Itraconazole x12 weeks total.

questions.question: A 60-year-old woman who is CMV-seropositive received a kidney from her CMV-seropositive husband for polycystic kidney disease.
questions.question_raw: 6. 60F something lady (CMV +) who received her husband's kidney (also CMV +) for polycystic kidney disease.

parts.text: Given her intermediate risk, list 2 acceptable management strategies to reduce her risk of CMV disease.
Give 1 advantage and 1 disadvantage of each modality.
She returns with fever, thrombocytopenia and diarrhea. CMV viral load is 56,000 copies/mL and colon biopsy shows CMV intracellular inclusions. List 2 first-line drugs to treat her condition.
For how long will you treat her?

parts_raw.text: Given her intermediate risk, list 2 acceptable management strategies to reduce her risk of CMV disease.
b) Give 1 advantage and 1 disadvantage of each modality

c) She comes back with fever, thrombocytopenia and diarrhea. Her CMV viral load is 56 000 copies/mL. A colon biopsy reveals CMV intracellular inclusions. List 2 drugs you can use as first line treatment for her condition.
d) For how long will you treat her?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Universal antiviral prophylaxis (e.g., oral valganciclovir post-transplant). (2) Preemptive therapy: serial quantitative CMV PCR monitoring with antiviral treatment when a threshold is reached. b) Prophylaxis - advantage: reduces CMV disease and indirect effects (rejection, secondary infections); disadvantage: drug toxicity/cost, risk of late-onset disease after stopping, and selection of drug-resistant virus. Preemptive - advantage: avoids drug exposure/toxicity in patients who never reactivate; disadvantage: requires intensive, reliable virologic monitoring and disease may develop before detection. c) (1) IV ganciclovir. (2) Oral valganciclovir (foscarnet if resistance/myelosuppression). d) Treat until clearance of viremia and resolution of symptoms, generally a minimum of 2-3 weeks.
questions.beyond_mandell: Specific 2-3 week minimum treatment duration follows AST/transplant ID guidance; Mandell states treatment continues until resolution of infection without giving a fixed interval.

cohort_answer.text: Strategies: 1. Preemptive therapy (weekly CMV blood PCR, treat if positive before symptoms/disease develop); 2. Prophylaxis with PO valganciclovir x3mos post transplant. Advantage/disadvantage: Preemptive therapy -> advantage: less likely to develop late disease, eliminate SE of anti-viral medication; disadvantage: requires diligent follow-up and risk of CMV disease developing. Prophylaxis -> advantage: proven to reduce CMV and other opportunistic infections and decreases risk of transplant rejection; disadvantage: SE of medication, cost, risk of developing CMV disease resistant to valganciclovir. First line for CMV colitis: IV ganciclovir, PO valganciclovir. Alternatives (2nd line): IV foscarnet. NB. Cidofovir has never been studied for CMV colitis. Duration: IV ganciclovir (or PO valganciclovir 900mg BID), minimum 2 weeks, generally 2-4 weeks, treat until clearance of viremia and no symptoms.

questions.question: A kidney transplant patient who works in the St. Lawrence river valley presents with fever, cough, bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. You suspect acute pulmonary histoplasmosis. There is no extrapulmonary disease.
questions.question_raw: A kidney transplant patient who works in the St-Lawrence river valley presents with fever, cough, and is found to have bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and mediastinal lymphadenopathy. You suspect acute pulmonary histoplasmosis. There is no extrapulmonary disease.

parts.text: What are the infection control precautions to take for this patient?
Understanding the transmission cycle of this organism, how could a healthcare worker acquire this infection?
Name two indications this patient has for receiving treatment.

parts_raw.text: What are the infection control precautions to take for this patient?
Understanding the transmission cycle of this organism, how could a HCW acquire this infection?
Name 2 indications this patient has for receiving treatment.

questions.model_answer: a) Routine/standard precautions – no person-to-person (pulmonary) transmission has been reported. b) By inhalation of aerosolized microconidia: in the environment when contaminated (bird/bat guano-enriched) soil is disturbed, or in the laboratory from sporulating mould-phase cultures – acquisition is by inhalation of the infective conidia, the same route as the patient. c) (1) Immunosuppression (transplant recipient), at risk of progressive disseminated disease. (2) Failure to improve after >1 month of illness or hypoxemia.
questions.beyond_mandell: The immunosuppression indication rests on the IDSA histoplasmosis guideline; Mandell text directly supports only the '>1 month/hypoxemia' criterion.

questions.question: A transplant candidate has the following pre-transplant serology results. What interventions, if any, would you provide for each result? Assume each result is independent of the others.
questions.question_raw: Pre-transplant transplant with various serology results (shown below). What interventions, if any would you provide for the following results? - assume each result is independent of the others.

parts.text: Toxoplasma IgG positive.
Hepatitis B surface antigen negative, core antibody positive, surface antibody positive.
Varicella-zoster virus IgG positive.
Herpes simplex virus IgG positive.

parts_raw.text: Toxo IgG positive
Heb sAG neg, core positive, surface antibody pos
Vzv igg positive
Hsv igg positive

questions.model_answer: a) Toxoplasma IgG positive indicates prior (latent) infection and risk of reactivation, most relevant in heart recipients (encystment in cardiac muscle). No pre-transplant treatment; provide routine post-transplant TMP-SMX prophylaxis, which covers both Toxoplasma reactivation and Pneumocystis. b) HBsAg-/anti-HBc+/anti-HBs+ is resolved HBV with natural immunity. Risk is reactivation under immunosuppression, greatest with B-cell-depleting therapy (rituximab). Intervention: monitor HBV DNA (and consider antiviral prophylaxis with entecavir/tenofovir) if rituximab or intensive immunosuppression is planned; no vaccination needed. c) VZV IgG positive means the patient is immune, so no varicella (Varivax) vaccine is required; offer the non-live recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) pre-transplant if age-eligible. d) HSV IgG positive indicates latent infection with reactivation risk; no pre-transplant intervention, provide post-transplant antiviral prophylaxis (acyclovir/valacyclovir, or coverage by valganciclovir CMV prophylaxis).
questions.beyond_mandell: Choice of entecavir/tenofovir for anti-HBc+ reactivation prophylaxis reflects AST/AASLD guidance; the chapter states only that rituximab is associated with HBV reactivation.

questions.question: A renal transplant recipient is CMV D+/R+ and received pre-transplant T-cell depletion.
questions.question_raw: PM Q15. Renal transplant with CMV D+/R+ and pre-transplant T-cell depletion

parts.text: What are 2 options for post-transplant CMV management?
What 2 agents could be used for these management options? (agent and route)

parts_raw.text: a) What are 2 options for post-transplant CMV mgmt.?
b) What 2 agents could be used for these management options? (agent and route)

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Universal antiviral prophylaxis (fixed-duration antiviral given to all at-risk recipients from the early post-transplant period). (2) Pre-emptive therapy (serial quantitative NAAT/antigenemia monitoring, with antiviral started only once a predefined viral threshold is reached).
b) (1) Valganciclovir PO (oral valganciclovir/ganciclovir are first-line for prophylaxis and treatment). (2) Ganciclovir IV (used when oral not tolerated or for treatment); T-cell depletion (ATG) can modify risk stratification upward.
questions.beyond_mandell: Letermovir PO/IV is an established SOT/HSCT prophylaxis agent (AST-IDCOP guidance); Mandell notes its HSCT prophylaxis role but says SOT use remains to be demonstrated.

cohort_answer.text:
Prophylaxis; pre-emptive with weekly CMV levels. Valganciclovir prophylaxis for 12 months in CMV seropositive/positive donor patients, particularly D+/R- highest risk
Both options x3 months (R+ status lower risk): Valganciclovir PO; Ganciclovir IV; Letermovir IV or PO

questions.question: A renal transplant recipient has acute histoplasmosis (mediastinal lymphadenopathy, reticulonodular findings, no extrapulmonary findings) with symptoms for 2 months, assuming the diagnosis is correct.
questions.question_raw: AM 26. Acute histo in renal transplant (mediastinal lymphadenopathy, reticulonodular findings, no extrapulmonary findings). Has had symptoms for 2 months.

parts.text: What precautions are needed for the healthcare worker?
What precautions are needed for the lab worker?
Given the life cycle, how could a healthcare worker become infected?
What are two indications for treatment in this patient?

parts_raw.text: Precautions needed for HCW, assuming correct diagnosis (1)
Precautions for lab worker (1)
Given the life cycle, how could a HCW become infected (1)
Two indications for treatment in this patient (2)

questions.model_answer: a) Routine/standard precautions – no person-to-person transmission. b) Biosafety Level 3 for propagating/manipulating the sporulating mould (mycelial) phase; use a biological safety cabinet when opening plates or performing aerosol-generating procedures. c) By inhalation of microconidia – from disturbed guano-enriched soil in the environment, or from sporulating mould cultures in the lab (the same inhalational route as the patient). d) (1) Immunosuppression (transplant recipient). (2) Symptoms persisting/not improving after >1 month (or hypoxemia).
questions.beyond_mandell: The immunosuppression treatment indication is per IDSA guidance; Mandell text grounds the '>1 month/hypoxemia' criterion directly.

cohort_answer.text: HCW precautions: Standard precautions (no person to person transmission). Lab worker: Biosafety level 3, use safety cabinet when opening plates or for aerosolizing procedures (CL3 organism must go to appropriate lab). HCW infection route: inhaling fungal spores in the environment or micro lab (same way patient did). Treatment indications: Immunocompromised; symptoms >1 month; Cavitary Pulmonary Histo, Progressive Disseminated Histo, Meningitis, Endocarditis.

questions.question: A renal transplant recipient with diabetes cut his hand at a lake house. One week later he developed papules and ulcerative lesions on the hand and arm without lymphatic involvement. Pathology shows granulomatous inflammation with a soccer-ball appearance (morulae); AFB and bacterial stains are negative. Sabouraud agar grows a white fluffy colony at 6 days.
questions.question_raw: Renal transplant, diabetic, and cut hand at lake house. 1 Week later got papules and ulcerative lesions on the hand and arm. There is no lymph involvement. Pathology shows granulomatous inflammation with soccer ball appearance (morulae). AFB and bacterial negative. Sabouraud agar shows white fluffy colony at 6 days.

parts.text: What is the most likely genus?
What group of organisms does this belong to?
What are two treatments?

parts_raw.text: What is the most likely genus?
What group of organisms does this belong to?
What are two treatment?

questions.model_answer: a) Prototheca (the morula/soccer-ball sporangia with internal endospores and water/lake exposure are characteristic; the absence of lymphatic spread argues against classic sporotrichoid disease). b) Achlorophyllous (colourless) green algae. c) (1) Amphotericin B (lipid formulation); (2) an azole - itraconazole or fluconazole (surgical excision of localized lesions is adjunctive).
questions.beyond_mandell: Protothecosis is not covered in this Sporothrix slice; morphology and therapy per standard Mandell/CMR protothecosis teaching.

questions.question: CMV in transplant.
questions.question_raw: CMV in transplant

parts.text: List and describe two methods for managing potential CMV infections.
What are two options for prophylaxis?

parts_raw.text: list and describe two methods for managing potential CMV infections.
What are two options for prophylaxis?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Universal prophylaxis – an antiviral is given to all at-risk recipients for a fixed duration from the early post-transplant period, regardless of viral load. (2) Pre-emptive therapy – serial quantitative virologic monitoring (NAAT or antigenemia) with antiviral started only once a predefined threshold of replication is detected, continued until viral clearance.
b) (1) Valganciclovir (oral) / ganciclovir (IV) – first-line. (2) Letermovir – non-myelosuppressive, established for high-risk HSCT prophylaxis.

questions.question: Vaccination timing in transplant recipients.
questions.question_raw: Transplant vaccines

parts.text: When is the earliest you can give inactivated vaccines pre-transplant?
When is the earliest you can give live-attenuated vaccines post-transplant?

parts_raw.text: When is the earliest you can give inactivated vaccines pre-transplant?
When is the earliest you can give live-attenuated vaccines post-transplant?

questions.model_answer: a) Inactivated (non-live) vaccines should be given as early as possible in the course of the illness before transplantation, since immunogenicity is higher before immunosuppression; there is no minimum interval, though ideally at least ~2 weeks before transplant. b) Live-attenuated vaccines are generally contraindicated after transplantation and should instead be completed before transplant (live vaccines require deferral of transplantation for 4 weeks after administration). Thus post-transplant they are essentially not given under standard practice.
questions.beyond_mandell: The ~2-week pre-transplant interval and emerging protocols allowing selected live vaccines (MMR/varicella) in low-immunosuppression recipients come from AST/pediatric guidance, not this chapter.

questions.question: A patient who has had a heart transplant presents with recurrent cellulitis.
questions.question_raw: Patient post heart transplant with recurrent cellulitis.

parts.text: What is the most common infecting organism?
What are 3 things you can do to try to minimize recurrence?

parts_raw.text: What is the most common infecting organism?
What are 3 things you can do to try to minimize recurrence?

questions.model_answer: a) Staphylococcus aureus — the single most common cellulitis pathogen on direct sampling (~50%), with group A streptococci next; in transplant recipients consider gram-negatives and Candida as well. b) (1) Staphylococcus aureus decolonization (nasal screening/mupirocin, chlorhexidine washes) to reduce carriage. (2) Meticulous skin/foot care — treat interdigital tinea pedis and manage any edema with support stockings. (3) Optimize/reduce net immunosuppression where feasible; consider antibiotic prophylaxis for frequent recurrences.
questions.beyond_mandell: S. aureus decolonization and immunosuppression reduction in transplant recipients are from transplant/IDSA guidance; the chapter addresses general cellulitis microbiology and prevention only.

cohort_answer.text: S. aureus most common (DDx: enterococci, GNB, Candida, M. hominis, rarely mucor/crypto). Minimize recurrence: screening nares for S. aureus decolonization pre-transplant, S. aureus decolonization, antibiotic prophylaxis; foot care (treat cutaneous fungal infections, cuts/bruises); reduce immunosuppression if possible; compression stockings if edema.

questions.question: Regarding post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD).
questions.question_raw: Regarding post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder:

parts.text: What are two risk factors for this condition?
What test can be performed on a lymph node biopsy that will support this diagnosis?

parts_raw.text: What are 2 risk factors for this condition?
What test can be performed on a lymph node biopsy that will support this diagnosis?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) EBV serostatus mismatch (EBV-seropositive donor / EBV-seronegative recipient, D+/R-). (2) Intense immunosuppression, particularly T-cell-depleting induction/anti-rejection therapy (antithymocyte globulin); belatacept also increases EBV-associated PTLD. b) Detection of EBV in the tissue, most specifically EBV-encoded RNA in situ hybridization (EBER) on the lymph node biopsy.
questions.beyond_mandell: EBER in situ hybridization as the confirmatory tissue test is standard pathology practice; the chapter establishes the EBV association but does not name the specific assay.

questions.question: A 33-year-old man undergoes orthotopic liver transplant and is found to have latent tuberculosis infection.
questions.question_raw: A 33 year old male undergoes an orthotopic liver transplant (OLT) and is found to have LTBI.

parts.text: Name two therapies for LTBI that are least likely to interact with calcineurin inhibitors, and the duration for each.

parts_raw.text: Name TWO therapies for LTBI that are least likely to interact with calcineurin inhibitors, and the duration for EACH.

questions.model_answer: (1) Isoniazid monotherapy for 9 months (INH is not a significant CYP3A inducer, so it minimally affects tacrolimus/cyclosporine levels; give pyridoxine). (2) Rifabutin-based therapy for 4 months — rifabutin is a much weaker cytochrome P-450 inducer than rifampin and is preferred over rifampin/rifapentine when a rifamycin is needed with calcineurin inhibitors (with calcineurin-inhibitor level monitoring). Rifampin/rifapentine-based regimens are avoided because of strong CYP3A induction and marked lowering of tacrolimus/cyclosporine levels.
questions.beyond_mandell: Selecting LTBI regimens specifically for minimal calcineurin-inhibitor interaction in transplant reflects AST/IDSA transplant-ID guidance; Mandell notes rifabutin is a weaker inducer and lists standard LTBI regimens (9 mo INH, 4 mo RIF).

questions.question: A 22-year-old person had a lung transplant 2 weeks ago and then presents in status epilepticus with an ammonia level of 1643 umol/L.
questions.question_raw: A 22 year old person had a lung transplant 2 weeks ago, and then presents in status epilepticus with an ammonia level of 1643 umol/L.

parts.text: Name TWO microorganisms that could cause this presentation.

parts_raw.text: Name TWO microorganisms that could cause this presentation.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Ureaplasma urealyticum (2) Ureaplasma parvum. Disseminated Ureaplasma infection is the recognized cause of the usually fatal hyperammonemia syndrome in immunocompromised patients, particularly lung transplant recipients; both Ureaplasma species have been implicated. These infections respond to appropriate antibiotics (azithromycin plus levofloxacin initially).
questions.beyond_mandell: Mycoplasma hominis (including donor-derived) is also reported to cause post-transplant hyperammonemia (Smibert et al., CID 2017) and is an acceptable alternative organism.

questions.question: Central nervous system infections in solid organ transplant recipients.
questions.question_raw:
Q20 (2011 PM)
CNS infections in SOT patients

parts.text: State the vulnerable windows post-transplant for each CNS pathogen.

parts_raw.text: A) Vulnerable windows post-transplant for each pathogen

questions.model_answer: a) Early (<1 month): CNS opportunistic infection is uncommon; consider nosocomial bacterial infection and donor-derived agents (West Nile virus, LCMV, rabies). Middle (1-6 months, peak risk for opportunistic CNS infection): Listeria monocytogenes and Nocardia (bacteria); Toxoplasma gondii; Aspergillus and agents of mucormycosis; HHV-6, VZV. Late (>6 months): Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis (characteristically a late, subacute event), JC virus (PML), West Nile virus, and Nocardia (can also occur late). Note that pyogenic bacteria and HSV are conspicuously absent from the transplant CNS pathogen list despite being common elsewhere.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort/H-decks timeline lists HSV encephalitis as a late CNS event, whereas Mandell's CNS pathogen table (308.11) specifically excludes HSV and pyogenic bacteria from CNS disease in transplant recipients.

cohort_answer.text:
<1 month: nosocomial (donor or recipient) infections - MRSA, VRE, Candida; aspiration, catheter infection, wound infection, anastomotic leaks, UTI, C diff; Donor derived (uncommon): HSV, LCMV, rhabdovirus, WNV, HIV, Trypanosoma; Recipient derived (colonization): Aspergillus, Pseudomonas.
1-6 months: With PCP and antiviral (CMV/HBV) ppx: Polyomavirus BK infection/nephropathy, C diff, HCV, Adenovirus, Influenza; Cryptococcus neoformans, TB. Without ppx: PCP, HSV, VZV, CMV, EBV, HBV; Listeria, Nocardia, Toxo, Strongyloides, Leishmania, T. cruzi.
>6 months: CAP, UTI; Aspergillus, atypical molds, mucor, nocardia, rhodococcus spp; Late viral: CMV colitis/retinitis, HBV, HCV, HSV encephalitis, WNV, JC PML, PTLD, skin CA.

questions.question: A renal transplant patient (CMV D+/R+) has fever and colitis, with WBC 3.4 and creatinine 126.
questions.question_raw: CMV in renal transplant patient (CMV D+/R+), patient has fever and colitis. WBC 3.4, Cr 126.

parts.text: 2 possible CMV prevention strategies.
1 advantage and 1 disadvantage of each.
With CMV PCR 56000, fever and colitis, give 2 first-line treatments in this patient and the duration of treatment.

parts_raw.text: 2 possible CMV prevention strategies
1 advantage and 1 disadvantage of each
CMV PCR 56000, fever, colitis. 2 first-line treatments in this patient, and duration of tx?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Universal antiviral prophylaxis (valganciclovir for a fixed post-transplant period). (2) Pre-emptive therapy (serial qPCR monitoring, treat when a threshold is reached).
b) Prophylaxis - advantage: simple, prevents reactivation and indirect CMV effects; disadvantage: drug toxicity/cost, risk of late-onset disease and selection of resistant virus. Pre-emptive - advantage: less overall drug exposure/toxicity and lower cost; disadvantage: requires frequent virologic monitoring and prevents disease rather than infection.
c) (1) IV ganciclovir and (2) oral valganciclovir are the first-line agents (IV ganciclovir preferred for severe/tissue-invasive disease). Treat until clinical resolution and viral clearance, a minimum of ~2 weeks.
questions.beyond_mandell: Specific dosing (ganciclovir 5 mg/kg q12h, valganciclovir 900 mg BID) and the 2-week/until-clearance treatment duration follow AST/IDSA transplant guidance; Mandell names the agents but not the exact regimen.

cohort_answer.text: A) Pre-emptive therapy (monitor CMV VL qweekly x12 weeks, treat if viremic); prophylaxis. B) Pre-emptive: advantage - effective agents also treat CMV disease, lower cost; disadvantage - frequent weekly bloodwork, agents myelosuppressive/nephrotoxic. Letermovir ppx: advantage - less myelo/nephrotoxic, lower rates of invasive CMV infection vs placebo; disadvantage - cost of daily tx, need to rule out active CMV disease (switch regimen), associated with late onset CMV disease. C) First line: IV Ganciclovir 5mg/kg q12h for severe/life-threatening disease, high VL or questionable oral absorption; PO Valganciclovir 900mg BID for mild-moderate disease. Duration until resolution of clinical symptoms and viral load undetectable, minimum 2 weeks; secondary ppx 1-3 months may be considered; caution reduction in immunosuppression especially if mod-severe disease.

questions.question: Vaccines in hematopoietic stem cell transplant and solid organ transplant patients.
questions.question_raw: Vaccines in HSCT/SOT transplant patients

parts.text: When is the earliest you can give inactivated vaccines pre-transplant?
When is the earliest you can give inactivated vaccines post-transplant?

parts_raw.text: When is the earliest you can give inactivated vaccines pre-transplant?
When is the earliest you can give inactivated vaccines post-transplant?

questions.model_answer:
a) Inactivated vaccines should be given at least 2 weeks before transplant (before the start of conditioning for HSCT, or before transplant/induction immunosuppression for SOT), so that the response is mounted while the patient is still relatively immunocompetent. Live vaccines require a longer interval — at least 4 weeks before conditioning or transplant. Ideally the full indicated schedule is completed during the pre-transplant assessment, as immunogenicity is much better before than after transplant.

b) HSCT: inactivated vaccines are restarted at 3 to 6 months post-transplant — influenza vaccine as early as 3–4 months (or 6 months, with a second dose if given earlier), and the routine re-immunization series (pneumococcal conjugate, Tdap-IPV-Hib, hepatitis B, meningococcal, HPV) generally beginning at 6 months. Live vaccines (MMR, varicella) are deferred to at least 24 months post-transplant and only if the patient is off immunosuppression, free of chronic GVHD, and immunocompetent. SOT: inactivated vaccines are given from 3 to 6 months post-transplant, once maintenance-level immunosuppression is reached and the patient is stable; influenza vaccine may be given as early as 1 month post-transplant during an outbreak or season. Live vaccines are generally contraindicated after SOT. Additional points: hepatitis B at double dose with serologic follow-up, HPV as a 3-dose series regardless of age, and recombinant zoster vaccine (non-live) is safe and indicated in both populations.
questions.beyond_mandell: AST Infectious Diseases Community of Practice vaccination guidelines and NACI Immunization of Immunocompromised Persons.

cohort_answer.text: A) Inactivated vaccines: at least 2 weeks before conditioning. Live attenuated vaccines: at least 4 weeks before conditioning. B) SOT: live vaccines not recommended post-SOT; inactivated vaccine wait 3-6 months post-transplant or when maintenance immunosuppression attained; HepB at double usual dose; HPV 3-dose schedule regardless of age. HSCT: live vaccine around 24 months post-transplant if immunocompetent and no GVHD; inactivated vaccine 6-12 months post-transplant; COVID (3 doses + boosters) can begin 3-6 months post-transplant.

questions.question: A transplant patient develops infection with histoplasmosis.
questions.question_raw: A transplant patient develops an infection with histoplasmosis.

parts.text: What are four immune phenomena you can get from histoplasmosis?
What are two other syndromes/infections with histoplasmosis?

parts_raw.text: What are 4 immune phenomenon you can get from histoplasmosis?
What are 2 other syndromes/infections with histoplasmosis?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Arthralgias/arthritis. (2) Erythema nodosum. (3) Erythema multiforme. (4) Pericarditis (inflammatory, from adjacent mediastinal nodes rather than direct invasion). Mediastinal granuloma/fibrosis is a further immune-mediated phenomenon. b) (1) Progressive disseminated histoplasmosis (with hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenias, mucosal ulcers, CNS/adrenal involvement). (2) Chronic cavitary pulmonary histoplasmosis; other syndromes include mediastinal fibrosis, endocarditis/endovascular infection and CNS (chronic meningitis) disease.

cohort_answer.text: Immune phenomena: Pericarditis, arthritis, erythema nodosum, erythema multiforme (rarely Histo actually cultured from pericardial/joint fluid, thought inflammatory rather than infected; note adrenal insufficiency in histo is actual tissue infection, not immunologic). Other syndromes: Chronic meningitis, chronic cutaneous, pulmonary, gastrointestinal, endocarditis presentations.

questions.question: EBV-associated post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease (PTLD).
questions.question_raw: EBV-associated PTLD

parts.text: What are 2 clinical risk factors for early PTLD after solid organ transplant?
What testing method do you use to identify EBV disease on lymph node biopsy?

parts_raw.text: What are 2 clinical risk factors for early PTLD after SOT (1)
What testing method do you use to identify EBV disease on lymph node biopsy (0.5)

questions.model_answer: a) Two risk factors: (1) primary EBV infection after transplantation (EBV D+/R- mismatch, seronegative recipient) - up to half of PTLD arises with primary infection and often in EBV-naive children; (2) intensity of T-cell immunosuppression, particularly T-cell-depleting therapy such as antithymocyte globulin (also higher-risk graft type, e.g. multivisceral/intestinal). b) In situ hybridization for EBV-encoded RNA (EBER) on the biopsy tissue demonstrating nuclear staining in tumour cells.

cohort_answer.text: Risk factors: Type of transplant (multivisceral high rates likely due to lymphoid tissue in transplant organs already heavily infected with EBV); Primary infection due to EBV mismatch (D+, R-); Degree of T cell immunosuppression; Time post-transplant (highest risk early in BMT where immunosuppression highest early on); Use of antithymocyte globulin; EBV-encoded small nuclear RNAs (EBERs) present in transplant organ; Late PTLD associated with chronic GVHD
